articles.title: PrivacyPal Mobile arrives on iPhone and iPad
articles.author: PrivacyPal Newsroom
articles.excerpt: The phone is where the sensitive prompt actually gets typed. PrivacyPal Mobile protects AI traffic on iOS and iPadOS, and by construction it never receives anything else.

body.text: For immediate release

WEST PALM BEACH, FL, October 1, 2026: PrivacyPal LLC (“PrivacyPal” or the “Company”), the premier on-device governance and security infrastructure for artificial intelligence, today announced PrivacyPal Mobile for iOS and iPadOS. Mobile carries the Company’s on-device interception to the handset, where it governs the AI applications an employee uses and, by deliberate architecture, never receives anything else.
The Desktop Design Did Not Survive Contact With iOS

On a laptop PrivacyPal owns the network path. A local proxy, a trusted certificate and a policy file are enough to see every request an AI client makes and to protect it before it leaves. iOS offers one comparable lever, a packet tunnel, and attaches three constraints to it: a hard memory ceiling measured in a handful of megabytes, no ability to draw an interface, and certificate trust that cannot be automated, deep-linked or even read outside of mobile device management.

A port of the desktop design would have failed on all three, and the failure mode is not a warning dialog. It is a dropped AI request the user experiences as the assistant being broken. So the Company inverted the model instead.
Scoped, Not Filtered

Rather than receiving all traffic and filtering out what does not matter, the tunnel claims routes only for the AI destinations under policy. Packets from a banking app are never handed to the extension at all: not filtered, not inspected, not seen. Five layers hold that boundary in place.

items: A denylist compiled into the binary that no downloaded policy can override.
Claimed routes limited to the AI ranges, so everything else leaves the device directly.
DNS matching limited to intercept hosts, so nothing else is even resolved through PrivacyPal.
A per-connection lease that encodes the destination hostname, so the governing policy is known before the connection opens rather than inferred once it is running.
A server-name cross-check at the TLS handshake, which catches any mismatch between the destination requested and the destination presented.

body.text: That yields a claim the desktop build cannot make. On iOS, PrivacyPal is structurally incapable of seeing a user’s non-AI traffic. For a security reviewer that is the difference between a policy promise and a property of the system, and it is the line the Company leads with in front of a CISO.
The Twin Engine Runs on the Handset

Protection itself happens on the phone. Sensitive spans are detected with Apple’s on-device natural language framework alongside checksum-validated detectors for email addresses, phone numbers, government identifiers, payment cards validated with Luhn, IBANs, addresses and postal codes. Each detected value is replaced with a twin that preserves its entity type, so a date still reads as a date and a customer name still reads as a name.

Twins hold steady inside a conversation and are deliberately not reused across conversations. A twin that persists forever becomes a tracking identifier, which would reintroduce the exact linkability the substitution exists to remove. Nothing about the detection pass leaves the device.

The phone is where the sensitive prompt actually gets typed. It is also the device where nobody will accept a security product that reads everything, and they are right not to. So we built a tunnel that is blind to every destination except the ones it is permitted to govern, and we do the protection work on the handset. We never wanted your traffic. Now we cannot have it.
What It Does Not Do
Four limits ship stated, because a security review finds them anyway and an optimistic coverage matrix does not survive one:

items: Siri, Apple Intelligence and Private Cloud Compute cannot be intercepted, by PrivacyPal or by anyone else. Apple’s transport is attested and much of it never touches the network. The only available control is an MDM restriction, and PrivacyPal claims nothing beyond that.

Always-On VPN in Apple’s sense is available only to IKEv2 profiles. What ships instead is on-demand connect rules on every interface, a non-removable configuration profile, and user VPN creation disabled. The outcome matches; the label does not, and the Company states it precisely rather than winning a checklist and losing the bake-off.
Preventing removal of the app requires a supervised device. On unsupervised hardware PrivacyPal detects removal within three minutes and reports it, but cannot block it.
Certificate-pinned applications are refused rather than passed through unprotected. A surface PrivacyPal cannot protect does not get a silent exception, on any platform.

body.text: Deployment and Availability

items: Managed fleets: distribution through Apple Business Manager custom apps, with a per-app VPN that scopes protection to the applications IT names.
BYOD: a packet tunnel scoped to the same AI routes, which leaves personal traffic untouched and demonstrably out of reach.
No in-app purchase of any kind. Seats are bought on the web, so Apple takes no commission and procurement stays where it belongs.
Android is in development and will be announced separately.

body.text: PrivacyPal Mobile is available beginning today through PrivacyPal and its distribution and managed-service partners. Deploy once. Govern the phone the same way you govern the laptop. Write to hi@privacypal.ai to arrange a pilot.

articles.title: PrivacyPal launches Family: guardrails for the AI kids already use
articles.author: PrivacyPal Newsroom
articles.excerpt: Approve the tools. Protect what gets typed. See how it is going without reading a word of it. PrivacyPal Family is $9.99 a month for five devices in the house.

body.text: For immediate release

WEST PALM BEACH, FL, September 21, 2026: PrivacyPal LLC (“PrivacyPal” or the “Company”), the premier on-device governance and security infrastructure for artificial intelligence, today announced the public launch of PrivacyPal Family, a consumer edition of its protection engine built for households. Family covers the AI tools children already use, protects the personal information that goes into them, and gives parents a view of what is happening without reading a word their child wrote. It is $9.99 a month for up to five devices.
The Gap Is Widest Where There Is No Governance at All

A company that deploys AI has an acceptable-use policy, a named owner, a defined integration scope, an audit trail and a regulator with a fine schedule. A fourteen-year-old with a chatbot has none of it. No policy applies. Nobody signed anything. The session runs at eleven at night on a bedroom laptop, and the only durable record of it sits with the model vendor.

The material is not trivial either. Into that box go a home address, a parent’s card number, the name of a school, a medical question the child would not ask out loud. Every argument the industry makes for governing AI inside a bank applies with more force to a household, which has no security team and no leverage with anyone.

The market’s existing answer is monitoring software: log the screen, read the messages, report upward. That trade buys the parent information at the child’s expense, and it has a short shelf life. Children route around surveillance, usually within a week, and what they learn from it is how to hide. PrivacyPal Family was built on the opposite premise. Guardrails, not surveillance.
Four Things Family Does

items: Guardrails. Parents approve, block or redirect AI tools per child and per device. A tool that has not been approved does not open, and the decision sits with the parent rather than with an app store rating.

Privacy Twins. When a child types a real name, address, phone number or card into an AI tool, PrivacyPal substitutes a coherent synthetic stand-in on the device before the prompt is sent. Structure and meaning survive the swap, so the model still answers the question properly. The real values never reach it.

Family Memory. What the household’s AI tools remember lives under the family’s own keys, stays visible in a viewer, and can be destroyed outright. Erasing the keys renders every copy unreadable, which is a mechanical guarantee rather than a deletion request that somebody else has to honor.

Pal Agents (early access). Wellbeing Signal flags when a conversation turns heavy and nudges a parent to check in. Answer Guard checks that an answer fits the child’s stage and blocks manipulation aimed at them, including prompt injection dressed up as a helpful instruction.

body.text: Signals, Never Transcripts

One rule governs the rest of the product. Parents see signals: which tools were used, how much, whether a guardrail fired, whether a conversation suggests it is time to check in. Parents do not see transcripts. Children can see exactly what their parents see, and that symmetry is not a setting that can be switched off.

The reasoning is practical rather than sentimental. A control a child understands is a control that survives contact with a teenager. A control that reads their diary teaches them to find a device that does not. Family protects the child and the relationship at the same time, and the Company treats the second one as a product requirement.
Autonomy That Moves With Age

Family ships a three-stage age ladder rather than a single on and off switch. Explorer covers ages 5 to 9, Navigator 10 to 13, and Pilot 14 to 17. Each stage widens what a child can do without asking first. At eighteen the keys hand over completely and the account becomes theirs, which is the point of the exercise. Parent HQ, the household dashboard, shows the whole family in one view.

We built the enterprise version of this first, and enterprises at least have rules. A kid has a chatbot, a laptop and no policy whatsoever. If the mechanism holds at that edge it holds anywhere, so Family runs the same engine we sell to banks, and the protection happens on your machine rather than in our cloud. You hold the keys. They get the future.
Pricing and Availability

items: $9.99 per month, up to five devices in the household.
Protected AI tools: ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and Grok, with new assistants covered as they arrive.
Mac and Windows are available today. iOS and Android are in early access.
Parent HQ and the Privacy Twins engine are included at every stage of the age ladder.
Founding Families receive 50 percent off the first year, applied at signup with the code sent with the invitation.

body.text: PrivacyPal also publishes a Child Psychology Guidebook for parents at privacypal.ai/family/guidebook.html, written to explain what changes when a child’s first research tool, tutor and confidant is a model. Wellbeing Signal and Answer Guard are labeled early access and are being rolled out to Founding Families first.
Set the guardrails at privacypal.ai/family. Hand over the keys later.

articles.title: PrivacyPal brings AI protection to headless Linux
articles.author: PrivacyPal Newsroom
articles.excerpt: Command-line AI agents run on servers with no browser, no window and, until now, no governance. The Linux Agent Shield protects them at the process boundary, before a packet leaves the box.

body.text: For immediate release

WEST PALM BEACH, FL, September 10, 2026: PrivacyPal LLC (“PrivacyPal” or the “Company”), the premier on-device governance and security infrastructure for artificial intelligence, today announced the PrivacyPal Linux Agent Shield, a command-line build of its interception engine for headless Linux. The Shield extends Privacy Twins protection to the AI agents that run where nobody is watching: Ubuntu and Fedora servers, build machines, and Windows Subsystem for Linux.
The Server Was the Blind Spot

Enterprise AI governance grew up around the screen. Nearly every control shipping today assumes a person at a laptop, a browser tab, a window that can be watched. That assumption held while AI was something employees typed into. It stopped holding the moment agents began running on their own.

A coding agent on a build server reads source files, executes commands, and posts the results to a model endpoint at three in the morning. The material is every bit as sensitive as anything a person would paste into a chat box: credentials, customer records, unreleased code. The difference is that no window ever opens, so the tooling built to catch it sees nothing at all. Surveys of enterprise AI risk keep landing on shadow AI as an employee behavior problem. On a server it is an architecture problem, and it does not respond to training.
What Ships

The Linux Agent Shield is a single privacypal command and a supervisor process, written in Python. There is no Electron, no desktop dependency and no graphical component anywhere in it. It runs the same interception engine as the PrivacyPal desktop application, unchanged:

items: Agent surfaces are covered. Hermes Agent, Claude Code, Codex, the OpenAI API and the xAI API are protected on the wire. Sensitive values are replaced with Privacy Twins before the request leaves the machine, and the model’s answer is translated back to real values as it returns.

Coverage is scoped by the operator, not imposed on the box. Protection attaches to an environment: launch an agent under privacypal run, work inside a protected privacypal shell, or export the settings into a shell of your own with one eval. No PAC file, no system proxy, no machine-wide setting. Every listener binds to loopback. A process you did not point at PrivacyPal is never touched by it.

Failure closes the door. If the encoder cannot be reached, the request stops rather than continuing in the clear. On this build a surface the license does not cover is refused on the wire instead of quietly passing through, a deliberate tightening of the desktop behavior.

One file installs it. A self-contained tarball of roughly 49 MB carries its own CPython 3.12.9 and pinned dependencies, installed by a user-level script. No root, no system Python, no dependency conflict with anything the server already runs. Builds ship for x86_64 and aarch64. Debian and RPM packages follow.

body.text: Verified on a Matrix, Not on a Slide

Every claim above was tested against the built artifacts on Ubuntu 24.04 and Fedora 40, on both architectures, before the release was published. The test that decides it is the wire audit: seeded sensitive values go into a live agent session, and the capture taken on the provider side of the connection is searched for them. They appear only as twins. The answers decode back to real values on the machine and nowhere else.

The same matrix covers an encoder outage (the request stops), a license lockout (the surface is refused at the wire), and a full install and uninstall cycle. The engine’s 1,435 unit tests run inside the bundled Linux runtime as part of the gate. A release that cannot clear the matrix does not get published.

Agents handle the most sensitive material in the building and they are the part of the stack nobody is watching. Yours reads your source, your keys and your customer records, then ships all of it to an API endpoint while the office is empty. You cannot govern that with a browser extension, because there is no browser. You govern it at the process boundary, on the machine, before the packet leaves.
Scope, Stated Plainly

The Shield covers agent surfaces only. Web chat platforms stay with the desktop application by design, because a headless server has no browser to protect. Coverage of Hermes Agent is scoped to the Nous Portal endpoint and the Fireworks endpoint Hermes uses by default; traffic pointed at another inference provider is not covered, and PrivacyPal states that limit rather than letting a customer discover it. The Shield is a PrivacyPal Max capability and rides the same release train as the desktop client.
The Linux setup guide is available to customers now. Point it at your agents. Write to hi@privacypal.ai to start.

articles.title: PrivacyPal launches Private Memory
articles.author: PrivacyPal Newsroom
articles.excerpt: Memory that follows you across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and Copilot. Secrets that don't. Opt-in, erasable, and born governed.

body.text: For immediate release

WEST PALM BEACH, FL, August 3, 2026: PrivacyPal LLC (“PrivacyPal” or the “Company”), the premier on-device governance and security infrastructure for artificial intelligence, today announced Private Memory: a user- and org-owned memory layer that follows you across ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Microsoft Copilot and custom agents, while the secrets underneath it never leave your control. With Private Memory, PrivacyPal expands from the protection layer of the AI operating system to its continuity layer.
The End of Walled-Garden Memory

Every major AI provider now ships memory, and every one of them is a walled garden. What ChatGPT learns about you stays with ChatGPT. Gemini builds its own profile. Copilot remembers inside the mailbox. Switch models and you start from zero; use three assistants and you maintain three strangers. The reason nobody has solved memory across providers is structural: whoever holds cross-provider memory holds the most sensitive longitudinal dataset in a person’s working life, and no model vendor is structurally trustable with it. PrivacyPal is built to be exactly that owner, because with Private Memory, the durable record never contains a real secret at all.
Memory Portability Without Memory Custody
Private Memory is built on the interception plane PrivacyPal already operates and the Privacy Twins architecture that made it the trusted boundary between enterprises and AI:

items: Captured where you already are. PrivacyPal’s on-device interception observes the full exchange, prompt and response, regardless of which model served it, with zero added latency in the hot path.

Stored in twin-space. Memories are distilled in the background and written to a bi-temporal memory graph that references synthetic twins, never real values. The real‐to‐twin map lives in an encrypted vault under the user’s own keys. PrivacyPal can host, sync and serve a memory it cannot read.

Injected into any model. At the moment of interception, relevant memory is assembled into a token-budgeted Memory Pack, with no LLM in the read path, and delivered to whichever AI the user is working in. New facts supersede old ones; contradictions are invalidated, never silently deleted.

Guarded at the write path. A dedicated Memory Guard quarantines instructions masquerading as facts, shipping a defense against memory poisoning, the emerging agentic attack class the OWASP agentic security taxonomy ranks among its most critical.

Erased by mathematics, not promises. Destroying a user’s vault keys renders every copy of their memory (synced, exported or cached) statistically plausible noise about entities that resolve to nothing. The right to be forgotten becomes a mechanical property of the architecture, not a data-deletion workflow.

body.text: Private Memory is opt-in and off by default. Users see, search and control what has been remembered, can exclude a conversation before it starts, and can erase everything, permanently, in one action.

Every AI vendor wants to own your memory, because whoever owns the memory owns the relationship. We built the version where you own it. Your memory follows you across every model on every device, and the secrets inside it don’t follow you anywhere, because they were never in the memory to begin with. That is what a trust layer beneath the AI Operating System is for.
PrivacyPal Max: Cross-Team, Cross-AI Collaboration. Born Governed

On PrivacyPal Max, the Company’s flagship enterprise edition, Private Memory becomes an organizational capability. Individual memory can be explicitly promoted, never silently harvested, into governed team and organization scopes, so knowledge established in one teammate’s Claude session is available, in twin-space, to another teammate’s Copilot. Max organizations get the full governance plane on top: org-wide memory policy, fleet-level Memory Guard controls, a complete audit console, and a Private MCP memory server that lets internal agents and tools query organizational memory without any connection leaking to a public host. Enterprises finally get what agent adoption has been missing: shared, cross-AI institutional memory without an ungoverned shadow database. Team and organization scopes are beginning their rollout to Max customers now.
Available Across the PrivacyPal Ecosystem

items: PrivacyPal Pro: personal cross-LLM memory, on-device, with full viewer, controls and incognito. Included with Pro, opt-in.
PrivacyPal Max: everything in Pro, plus governed team and org memory scopes, policy plane, Memory Guard fleet policies, Private MCP memory server and audit console. Rolling out now.
PrivacyPal Cloud, the sovereign memory plane: in-VPC deployment, bring-your-own-key, air-gap support, Memory DSPM and data residency.
PrivacyPal SDK, remember() and recall(): compliant cross-LLM memory for any application in two calls.

articles.title: Introducing Privacy Twins 2.0: synthetic substitution in real time
articles.author: PrivacyPal Newsroom
articles.excerpt: A new generation of on-device models replaces sensitive values with coherent, context-preserving synthetic data, so the model still understands the prompt, and the secret never leaves.

body.text: Redaction breaks the prompt. Replace a customer's name with [REDACTED] and the model loses the thread; replace a transaction with black bars and the analysis falls apart. Privacy Twins 2.0 takes a different path: it substitutes sensitive values with coherent synthetic equivalents that preserve meaning, structure, and relationships, so the model still does its job, and the real data never crosses the boundary.
What's new

items: Context-aware substitution that keeps entities consistent across a whole conversation.
A faster on-device detection model with broader coverage of regulated data types.
Reversible mapping under policy, so authorized workflows can re-link results downstream.
Full audit of every substitution: what was detected, what was swapped, and why.

body.text: The goal was never to hide data from the model. It was to give the model something just as useful that happens to be safe.
Privacy Twins 2.0 is rolling out to all customers over the coming weeks, on by default for new policies.

articles.title: PrivacyPal launches on Windows 11 and macOS
articles.author: PrivacyPal Newsroom
articles.excerpt: On-device protection arrives natively on the desktop: real-time Privacy Twins on Windows 11 and macOS, governed by a single policy and live in about a minute.

body.text: Today PrivacyPal is available natively on Windows 11 and macOS. The same real-time Privacy Twins that protect every AI interaction now run on the desktop, substituting sensitive data on-device, before a single token ever reaches a model.

Both builds are signed and notarized (a trusted publisher on Windows, notarized by Apple), so there are no scary first-launch dialogs. Drop it in, sign in, and your AI guardrails work everywhere in about a minute.
What you get on day one

items: Native builds for Windows 11 and macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel).
Real-time, on-device Privacy Twins across every AI app and browser tab.
One policy for the whole fleet: write it once, enforce it on every endpoint.
Zero-touch distribution through your existing MDM, with sub-10ms p95 overhead and full audit on.

body.text: Protection has to live where the work happens. For most teams that's the desktop, so that's where we made it effortless.
Download for Windows or macOS from the home page, or roll it out across your organization from the admin console today.
